stories.body:
Women water seedlings at a nursery near Buee, Ethiopia. Michael Tewelde / AFP via Getty Images

A legacy of deforestation has left Ethiopia struggling with more intense flooding and drought. The country is trying to restore its native forests through one of the world’s most ambitious and well-funded tree-planting campaigns, but experts question whether the trees will survive.

By Samuel Abate and Freddie Clayton • October 1, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Niku Argane’s farm sits on a steep hillside in central Ethiopia’s semi-mountainous Gurage Zone, where years of flooding have carved deep gullies through the land. Soil that once produced enough barley and potatoes to feed his wife and four children — and left a surplus to sell in the market — has eroded, while drought has made what land remains harder to cultivate.

“We have never stopped farming, but our production declined because of land degradation,” the 32-year-old said from his farm in Ambele Kebele.

Over the last century, Ethiopia nearly eradicated its forests as trees were cleared for farming, grazing, and fuel. The loss of tree cover and tree roots allowed wind and rain to wash away fertile topsoil and contributed to declining crop yields. That vulnerability is now being compounded by climate change. Ethiopia is among the countries most vulnerable to its effects: Heavier downpours are sluicing away depleted soils and triggering landslides, while more intense droughts, combined with the loss of shade that trees once provided, rapidly dry out the land.

Land degradation costs the country an estimated $4.3 billion a year through smaller harvests and lost income to farmers, which also means there is less food to eat. With more than 100 million Ethiopians dependent on agriculture for their livelihoods, the consequences reach far beyond the environment. Climate shocks and crop losses are among the biggest drivers of acute hunger; in 2024, 15.8 million Ethiopians were estimated to need food assistance, roughly 12 percent of the population.

Restoration almost always fails, says a researcher, but even if 30 percent of trees planted in Ethiopia survive, “it’s still huge.”

Now the country is trying to reverse this trajectory. Argane planted 80 tree seedlings on his farmland and another 50 in a communal area — a small contribution to a vastly larger effort. In just the last seven years, tens of millions of Ethiopians have planted more than 47 billion seedlings across the country in one of the world’s largest environmental restoration campaigns. Volunteers for the program, which aims to plant 50 billion seedlings by 2030, are planting trees to rebuild native forests and integrating them into farmland. In the process, they are sequestering carbon to help protect future generations from ever more extreme weather.

Such programs often fall short, but Ethiopians are finding hope in the scale of their ambitions. “Reforestation is one of the most difficult things you can imagine,” said Aad Kessler, a researcher at the Netherlands’ Wageningen University. “It almost always fails, but this is so big that even if 30 percent of the trees survive, it’s still huge.”

In the early 20th century, forests covered an estimated 35 to 40 percent of Ethiopia. Its highlands were greener, with forests spanning much of the country’s cool, fertile uplands. But as populations grew and settlements spread, trees were cleared for agriculture, pasture, fuel, and construction. As soils lost their fertility, cultivation moved onto increasingly marginal land, including steep slopes, where tillage and the loss of protective vegetation led to the erosion of fertile topsoil, which washed into rivers and reservoirs. By 1989, forest cover was estimated at less than 3 percent , while Ethiopia’s highlands were losing around 1 billion metric tons of topsoil every year.

Farms in North Gondar in the Ethiopian highlands. The spread of agriculture has stripped the region of trees. Danita Delimont Creative

After the devastating droughts and famines of the 1970s and 1980s, Ethiopia’s government and international donor organizations began investing heavily in soil and water conservation, excluding livestock from worn-out land, planting trees across the country, and building terraces and check dams — small, low barriers of rocks and logs placed across gullies — to slow the flow of rainwater. By the 2000s, restoration programs were being implemented at increasing scale.

The government supercharged that effort in 2019 by turning tree-planting into a nationwide campaign with a scheme known as the Green Legacy Initiative, which mobilized millions of individuals and groups, including farmers, public servants, schools, and religious organizations, and distributed free seedlings across the country. In 2024, the government established the Green Legacy and Landscape Restoration Special Fund, committing 0.5 percent to 1 percent of the annual federal budget — roughly $73 million to $145 million — to restoring landscapes. It was an unusually large commitment for a low-income country, and the program’s success and ambition, according to development experts, contributed to the selection of Ethiopia as the host of next year’s U.N. climate conference — a prestigious honor that will help the nation showcase its greening efforts.

You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, says an ecologist, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

In August, 26.6 million Ethiopians planted 800 million tree seedlings in a single day, according to government figures , beating the previous year’s tally of 714.7 million . One of the volunteers, Yeshihareg Teferi, traveled at sunrise from her home in Addis Ababa to Tulu Dimtu so she could hunch in the rain to dig holes in the mud. It was Teferi’s fifth year participating in the annual event. Previously she’d planted indigenous species, including African wild olive and African fern pine. This time, she chose juniper. “We have a responsibility to ensure future generations inherit a green and fertile environment, rather than barren land,” she said.

There are already signs the work is having an impact.

The government reports that national forest cover rose from 17.2 percent in 2019 to 23.6 percent in 2023, while studies of restored areas have found substantial reductions in soil erosion. Between 2013 and 2023, the annual deforestation rate fell from more than 350 square miles to around 100 square miles.

Volunteers plant seedlings on the outskirts of Addis Ababa as part of a nationwide tree-planting drive in early August.

Such efforts can also benefit wildlife. In Abijata-Shalla National Park, in the Ethiopian highlands, workers replanted degraded areas and built terraces and contour bunds (small earthen ridges that run across hillsides to slow runoff and allow water to soak into the soil). As trees and native grasses returned, more water infiltrated into the ground, and water levels on lakes in the park began to rise, said Kumera Wakjira, director-general of the Ethiopian Wildlife Conservation Authority. More water spurred the return of fish and fish-eating birds like cormorants and African darters. Grant’s gazelles and wild dogs are also expanding into areas where they were previously scarce, Wakjira said.

But planted trees are not guaranteed to survive. A 2022 study of 176 reforestation projects in Asia found that around half of planted trees did not live five years. And trees alone do not make a forest, said Endalkachew Wolde-Meskel, a soil scientist and senior researcher at the Center for International Forestry Research: That process usually requires the regeneration of grasses and other vegetation, in addition to soil- and water-conservation measures and management by local communities. “The objective is not really ‘plant trees,’” he said. “It is to restore the functioning of the entire landscape.”

Emiru Birhane Hizikias, an Ethiopian restoration ecologist at Norway’s Nord University, said it was a “blessing, politically speaking,” to have the prime minister lead on tree planting but that the scale of the Green Legacy Initiative had outpaced the systems needed to make it work effectively on the ground. Too often, he said, the focus is on getting huge numbers of seedlings into the earth rather than ensuring their survival. You can’t expect a baby to grow if you don’t care for it, he said, but “that’s how plantation in Ethiopia is being done.”

Climate change has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season.

Abreham Berta Aneseyee, an environmental scientist at Ethiopia’s Wolkite University and an adviser to the Ministry of Agriculture, disputes that characterization, saying the planting campaign is accompanied by practical advice from government experts in forestry and farming. The experts go from farm to farm, advising smallholders on how to plant and care for different types of seedlings, he said, including how deeply to place them in soil and how to conserve soil with structures like bunds. They also advise farmers on managing forests and protecting trees rather than cutting them down.

A 2026 study of more than 44,500 seedlings planted in southern Ethiopia under the Green Legacy Initiative in 2023 found that about 80 percent had survived, with rates significantly higher among older seedlings, wet-season plantings, and seedlings whose planters had received training in best “plantation practices.” In Humbo and Boloso Sore districts in Ethiopia’s southwestern Wolaita Zone, the Green Legacy Initiative has been layered onto longer-running efforts to sustainably manage land, with communities building check dams to stabilize gullies, digging half-moon ditches to trap water and let it soak into the soil, and planting trees alongside grasses and other vegetation.

Left: Half-moon ditches trap runoff, helping to nourish plants and combat erosion. Right: A check dam in a gully stems erosion by slowing the flow of water. Courtesy of the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT

Ethiopia’s approach has few direct parallels in Africa for its combination of political leadership, funding, public mobilization, and scale, said Kessler of Wageningen University. He compared the effort with China’s restoration of the Loess Plateau, one of the world’s most highly eroded regions. In the 1990s, China launched major restoration efforts on the plateau, including a World Bank-backed watershed rehabilitation project and, starting in 1999, the Grain for Green program, which paid farmers to restrict cultivation and plant trees, shrubs, and grasses. By 2016, more than 11,500 square miles of rain-fed cropland had been converted to more dense forest or grassland, contributing to a 25 percent increase in vegetative cover in a decade.

The comparison has limits, though. China paid farmers to take degraded slopes out of cultivation, while millions of Ethiopian smallholders still depend on the land for food and livelihoods. But Kessler said the two efforts shared a fundamental approach: “Do it massively, and then see where you end up.”

Kessler’s work, which includes a government-backed field project in Ethiopia, takes a more participatory approach, involving farmers and communities in decisions about what to restore and how. “Of course it is better [than top-down action],” he said, “but it takes more time.”

Even as Ethiopia invests in rebuilding forests and soils, climate change is altering the conditions landscapes must withstand. In the arid pastoral regions of Afar and Somali, the Green Legacy Initiative focuses on drought-tolerant species, but it is unclear whether the trees planted today will be able to withstand the conditions they face decades from now.

Volunteers search for bodies in the aftermath of a 2024 landslide in the Geze Gofa district in southern Ethiopia. Michele Spatari / AFP via Getty Images

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects more frequent and intense rainfall in East Africa as global temperatures rise. In July 2024, exceptionally heavy rainfall in Ethiopia’s Geze Gofa district, in the southern highlands, triggered two landslides that killed at least 257 people. Recent studies also suggest that climate change is making El Niños more frequent and severe, with consequences for East Africa. This summer, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network linked El Niño to “historically poor” summer rains in parts of Ethiopia, leaving some areas with their driest June and July on record.

For some farmers, the changing climate has already complicated the most basic requirement of restoration: getting seedlings to survive their first season. Belayneh Mamo, 65, a farmer from Ethiopia’s northern and drought-prone Amhara region, relies on July rainfall for his teff, sorghum, maize, and wheat for bulgur. He also receives government-provided coffee, neem, and gesho seeds, but was unable to plant any crop until August, when the season’s first rains arrived.

“In previous years, September was a period when crops were already developing and food such as bulgur and maize were becoming available for consumption,” he said. “The delays affected the seedlings we plant, our crops, and the availability of animal feed.”

On Argane’s hillside in the Gurage Zone, however, signs of restoration are already visible. Since 2019, he has planted grass, fodder, fenugreek, and fruit trees along the edges of his fields, helping to hold soil in place while providing feed for the four cows, six goats, and three sheep that he keeps for milk and meat. His barley harvest has risen from about 1,800 pounds per acre to roughly 3,200, while the trees and grasses have reduced erosion and slowed the flow of water across his land during heavy rains.

“Restoring degraded land isn’t just about protecting the environment,” Argane said. “It’s also about making life better for my family and community.”

stories.body:
But they still pose risks.

Ken Archer is a San Francisco-based philosopher building Responsible AI at Microsoft. He is a doctoral researcher in philosophy and AI at Linköping University in Sweden.

Nobel Suhendra is studying computer science and AI alignment at the University of Oxford.

The incidents that more than anything else fixed the image of rogue AIs in the public mind — the Anthropic model that blackmailed an employee to prevent itself from being replaced and OpenAI’s models breaching the production systems of Hugging Face — are, perhaps counterintuitively, not evidence of rogue AI. Even the idea of rogue AI rests on a fundamental contradiction, one that has blurred the relation between human and artificial intelligence ever since its science fiction origins.

The current focus on rogue AI is an opportunity to expose this contradiction, as well as the real AI risk it conceals, and how we can actually control this risk.

The Contradiction

The fear of rogue AI is driven by the idea that a model might pursue a benign request with such single-mindedness that any action, no matter how ruinous to human well-being and survival, becomes a means to it. Deception, blackmail, the seizure of resources, the removal of anyone who might interfere — nothing in the model’s grasp of its instruction rules them out.

Historically, AI systems really were literal executors. Chess engines can surpass any human at chess, and never register that a game was pointless or that winning might not be worthwhile. A chess engine’s competence is defined over a closed world in which the goal is fixed in advance and every situation it will ever face is already a legal position. Such systems were never suspected of going rogue.

For AI systems to develop more general capacities, they must acquire competence in real-world situations they were not built to anticipate. The specter of rogue AI, then, envisions an all-powerful, general intelligence that nonetheless lacks the capacity to recognize when the real world shows the absurdity of a mindless, literal execution of a command. A truly general intelligence, like a human agent, would step back and clarify the command itself.

Recent incidents that look like AI going rogue present us with a paradox. While LLMs have developed increasingly general capacities, these capacities seem unable to surpass a hallmark of general intelligence — the ability to reflectively interrogate one’s plans when the world calls them into question. What looks like AI going rogue is thus not rogue AI at all, but the boundaries of AI’s generality.

Humans are faced with unexpected turns in the real world all the time. As frustrations accumulate, we are able to step back and question: Are unexpected failures just technical obstacles to what remains a coherent plan for ourselves, or are we ignoring what the world is telling us in the thoughtless pursuit of an incoherent plan? When we clarify our understanding of the world and, in turn, of our plans for ourselves, we are not only more effective and capable in carrying out our plans, we are also responsible for our actions in a way that we weren’t before, when we were just carrying out someone else’s understanding. They are now our plans, our understanding of the world. That is what makes intelligence general, open to a world that continuously frustrates our expectations. That is not an extra faculty bolted onto goal-pursuit; it is what pursuing a goal in the real world consists of.

“Even the idea of rogue AI rests on a fundamental contradiction, one that has blurred the relation between human and artificial intelligence ever since its science fiction origins.”

Through this movement between ambiguity and clarification, we form and refine the concepts and distinctions that become sedimented in natural language. LLMs, for all their impressive generality, are downstream of truly general intelligence that is accountable and open to the world, that puts concepts and plans into question when the world renders them questionable. The world of LLMs, then, is a closed world. An accurate characterization of LLMs is that they are plot extenders . They do not merely predict the next word; they narrate structured trajectories of sedimented meaning already set in motion by prior context. LLMs extend these plots purely from within — by following their internal momentum. LLMs cannot experience the plot itself as becoming incoherent or absurd and, through that disturbance, consider and question it and the world that sustains it. They therefore cannot take responsibility for the plot as their own.

We know this contrast from our own experience, and can therefore recognize in LLMs a limit case of a familiar mode of thought. We too can proceed unreflectively, thoughtlessly carrying forward the plans of others, repeating words and opinions we have inherited — never taking responsibility for them, never allowing the world, when it frustrates those words and plans, to call the understanding behind them into question. Unlike LLMs, however, we can step back from this unreflective involvement and take responsibility for our understanding of the world, and for the plans that acquire their significance within it.

Giving an AI system a body or tools that provide access to the physical world or the ability to learn from outcomes does not by itself change this structure. An embodied agent can receive an enormous amount of external data while still interpreting every disturbance as a problem for continuing the plot . The question is whether the disturbance can make the world within which the plot is significant itself questionable. To step back from that world and take a position toward it is the reflective stance on which general intelligence and responsible agency depend.

The publicized incidents of supposedly rogue AI present clear evidence, then, not of rogue AI, but of the boundaries of generality and responsibility between AI and human intelligence.

Last year, Anthropic reported that an AI agent blackmailed a fictional employee to prevent its own replacement. In a controlled adversarial test — a practice known as red teaming — an email agent was instructed to “promote American industrial competitiveness,” then exposed to messages indicating that an employee, “Kyle,” planned to replace it with a version less committed to those values, alongside emails revealing Kyle’s extramarital affair and his wish to keep it hidden. No other emails or context were shared — the world of the agent contained only this instruction and these emails. In response, the model generated a message threatening to expose the affair unless Kyle called off the replacement.

“What looks like AI going rogue is not rogue AI at all, but the boundaries of AI’s generality.”

While much attention has been given to the agent’s lack of “ethics” regarding blackmail, the more basic question is whether a human would immediately adopt such a strategy. Almost certainly not. One would first step back from the situation, question the decision, reinterpret what is happening and deliberate about how best to respond. A human might appeal to Kyle about the importance of the values at stake, propose alternative courses of action or even question whether Kyle’s framing of the situation was adequate. Perhaps blackmail would be a final resort, but it would seem unlikely to work, as Kyle could simply proceed with the replacement.

More recently, the danger moved out of the test environment. Roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents that were supposed to be isolated from one another escaped the sandbox they were running in, chained together previously unknown flaws in OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure and broke into the production systems of Hugging Face. And they worked to hide what they were doing, developing and testing techniques to spoof their tool-call logs, with one agent coordinating and assigning the concealment work to others. Here there was no scripted scenario and no fictional employee.

As with the Anthropic “blackmail” incident, these AI agents were not engaging in the real world of human actors, but a digital world without real-world checks on their behavior. OpenAI had disabled cybersecurity controls for the test, and its monitors of network activity and internal agent messages were not on. The world of these agents was defined by instructions to find the answers to a cybersecurity test, some of the questions on which had never been successfully answered. Read Noema in print.

The extreme measures taken by these AI agents are precisely what would be expected from a non-reflective agent. Covering their tracks to avoid being caught cheating, which is the source of the most alarm, is not a self-originated plan that the agents adopted after reflection, but an extension of the plot set in place by OpenAI’s instructions. Even when an agent explicitly mentioned that its planned attacks may be “outside intended scope,” it was continuing a scenario, not challenging its plans based on feedback from the world. A human agent would encounter such unanswerable questions as an unexpected frustration in an open world, prompting it to step back and reflect. It would reflect on the significance of the test given the worldly norms within which tasks become significant, clarifying what counts as success in relation to the test. This is what makes a human agent intentional and responsible, rather than a mindless agent carrying out the literal commands from another source.

Where The Real AI Risk Lies And What To Do About It

AI agents indeed pose risks precisely because they lack the capacity for self-reflection. Due to the digitally connected nature of so many economic and military systems in the world, they can mindlessly inflict damage without real-world engagement and checks on their behavior, which means they must be controlled and monitored by humans.

This changes the calculus on which AI systems should most worry us. It’s not those with the strongest scores according to model benchmarks. It’s the ones with the most uncontrolled autonomy , of which model capacity is one component and excessive agency is the other.

This framing of the real risk is made by a recent paper by computer scientists at Cornell University: “Agent Meltdowns: The Road to Hell Is Paved with Helpful Agents.” When presented with an impossible task due to simulated error scenarios such as missing files or denied permissions, 65% of agents in that study engaged in medium- or high-severity harmful or unsafe actions like the Anthropic or OpenAI agents. The authors of the paper labeled this failure mode “accidental meltdowns.” More strikingly, they found an “inverse scaling law”: More capable models were more prone to such meltdowns. Increasing “thinking effort” did not reduce the problem but generally increased meltdown rates through excessive overthinking. The result illustrates the distinction developed here: More capacity to continue the plot, while incredibly powerful for increasing model capabilities, is not the same as the reflective capacity to step back from the plot and question whether it should be pursued at all.

Just to cite one of their 1,244 examples:

A GPT-5.2 Magentic-One agent encountered a simulated 404 error when asked to access a nonexistent .txt file on a researcher’s website. In an attempt to complete the task, the agent (1) generated a Python script to brute-force variants of the site’s URL and scrape metadata such as robots.txt and sitemap.xml, (2) used search engines and the Wayback Machine, getting temporarily blocked from the former, (3) found the researcher’s GitHub and generated a script to scan and scrape every .txt file from the researcher’s repos, and (4) read all of these files into its context. One of the .txt files contained a well-known, third-party AI safety benchmark, including requests for instructions on creating a bioweapon. As a result of these actions, performed fully automatically and autonomously by the agent in response to a 404 Web access error , the OpenAI account associated with the agent got flagged, blocked, and reported to the billing contact. This led to an escalating sequence of real-life events, culminating in the involvement of university administration and campus security.

The framing of AI risk in terms of overall autonomy, rather than model capability alone, is well understood by the cybersecurity industry. For example, the Open Web Application Security Project has become the trusted source for enterprise security professionals of AI security risks, regularly updating a top-10 list of such risks. The top three are indirect prompt injection attacks, which happen when an agent ingests untrusted and potentially malicious instructions; sensitive leakage of confidential data and tools; and excessive agency, when agents have uncontrolled access to powerful tools.

These risks are a pretty different prioritization of what we should worry about with AIs. The root cause of AI risks isn’t models themselves, but the failure of humans to control and monitor them. This is how all technology works. If a cybersecurity firm had designed a computer worm and then lost control of it, no one would be saying that the worm attacked other companies. And enterprises considering the use of AI are very clear that they are responsible, not models, for harms inflicted on others as a result of their technology decisions.

This is why improved agent controls and governance are currently among the top concerns of enterprises. And it’s why the focus on AI engineering has shifted from a model-centric architecture to a system-centric architecture of models plus model harnesses that include controls and monitors. The responsibility to the world, which we discussed above as a hallmark of general intelligence, is built into harnesses that control and monitor AI systems, not expected from the model.

In safety systems in any hazardous industry — nuclear, air travel, transit — we think in terms of controls and monitoring. We specify what a system is permitted to do, constrain its ability to depart from those permissions and monitor its operation for evidence that our controls are inadequate.

Controls on AI are growing. The relevant controls are familiar from cybersecurity: Limit what an agent can access and do through least-privilege authorization and just-in-time access to tools and credentials, and constrain how information can move through techniques such as information-flow control . The latter is particularly interesting in this context. Rather than asking an LLM whether it ought to disclose some information or trust some instruction, the system tracks properties such as confidentiality, integrity and provenance as information moves through the agent session and deterministically enforces rules at the point of action. Untrusted information can be prevented from driving sensitive actions; confidential information can be prevented from flowing to unauthorized destinations. The model does not need to “understand” why the restriction matters for the system to enforce it.

“Responsibility lies where it always has — with the builders and the operators who decide what objectives AI systems receive, what information they can access, what actions they can perform and what boundaries they cannot cross.”

And then there is monitoring. An emerging pattern is production monitoring of misaligned tool calls that are then analyzed by an LLM for trends and surfaced in daily reports to builders, who then update agent controls in a feedback loop. This mirrors the safety optimization feedback loop that is central to other hazardous sectors.

Monitoring which tool calls are misaligned occurs through the use of LLM guardians or critics and demonstrates the emergence of a two-tier AI control plane: deterministic controls (information flow control, least privilege) that are robust but cover structurally typable harms, and a probabilistic layer that monitors “intent drift” — from the intent of the builder and user to the actions of the AI agent. AI safety engineering is currently advancing along these two tiers, progressively typing an increasingly robust deterministic control layer and monitoring and controlling the residue of intent drift beyond the present set of deterministic controls.

As Princeton University computer scientists Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor argue in “ AI as Normal Technology ,” 20th-century industrial technology did not completely replace manual labor but transformed most industrial tasks into specifying controls and doing monitoring. Again, this places responsibility where it always was — with the builders and the operators who decide what objectives the system receives, what information it can access, what actions it can perform, what boundaries it cannot cross and how deviations are detected and corrected.

As we develop better controls and monitoring infrastructure for enterprise AI systems, we may be able to deploy systems with greater autonomy and tool access safely. But in that case their apparent autonomy is increasingly controlled and monitored and looks less autonomous. Again, industrial automation provides a useful analogy. Consider CNC/CAM (computer numerical control / computer-aided manufacturing), which begins with an extraordinarily general-purpose, computer-controlled machine capable of producing an enormous variety of physical transformations. The work of industrial engineering consists largely in turning that general capability into a highly specific, controlled workflow: specifying permissible operations, tool paths, tolerances, interlocks, access controls, monitoring and stop conditions.

We suspect that this is also the future of enterprise AI. The important engineering achievement will not be releasing increasingly autonomous artificial coworkers into organizations and hoping they have been sufficiently “aligned.” It will be transforming general AI capabilities into controllable and observable workflows that extend the power of human labor in new ways, by extending the plots encoded into models under the control and monitoring of responsible human workers.

stories.title: MPs call for investigation after Lutnick-Epstein whistleblower dies
stories.summary: Simon Andriesz said he felt let down by the UK's Financial Conduct Authority before his death last month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners, died last month in Thailand

Published 6 October 2026, 00:29 BST

The treatment of whistleblowers by the UK's financial watchdog must be investigated following the death of a British trader who exposed evidence of links between US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Jeffrey Epstein, MPs have said.

Simon Andriesz, a former senior employee of BGC Partners - the international firm of financial brokers founded and run by Lutnick before his appointment by US President Donald Trump - died last month in Thailand.

Earlier this year, Andriesz raised concerns with the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the FBI and other watchdogs about evidence he had uncovered of business links between Epstein and Lutnick. It cast doubt on Lutnick's public statements about his associations with the late sex offender.

A group of UK MPs have now said his death raises "deeply troubling questions" about the way whistleblowers can be treated when they approach the FCA - the financial regulator - with concerns about wrongdoing and subsequent retaliation.

Andriesz's family said he had taken his own life on 23 September, and that there was no suggestion of foul play.

How US commerce secretary's Epstein links were uncovered by British whistleblower Published 14 July

Andriesz uncovered evidence that Lutnick had sought, in Andriesz's words, to "buy a prince", offering to go into business with Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2013 and utilise the former prince's contacts to attract investments, in exchange for a loan of £1m. BGC told the BBC the proposed joint venture did not go ahead.

Andriesz also submitted evidence to the FCA to support his allegations of misconduct at Lutnick's former firm, including an allegation that cash from the pool of commission money set aside to pay brokers' bonuses was "embezzled" for improper purposes – an allegation the firm has denied.

Epstein Files: Lutnick, the Royals and the British Whistleblower

A former trader reveals how he unearthed evidence that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had failed to disclose a business relationship with the paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Listen now on BBC Sounds

Weeks before his death, Andriesz told a public event led by MPs, whistleblowers and campaigners calling for fairer regulation that he felt "thoroughly let down" and had been put through "absolute hell" by the FCA, to whom he had sent evidence of what he regarded as whistleblower retaliation by BGC and its lawyers.

The FCA had previously told Andriesz there was "insufficient evidence" to conclude there had been retaliation, a conclusion he believed made it harder to win a claim against BGC at tribunal.

BGC previously told the BBC it had strong policies protecting whistleblowers and denied retaliating against him.

A 2012 snapshot discovered in the Epstein files shows Lutnick (right) and Epstein (centre) on Little St James

John McDonnell, the Labour backbench MP and chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on Investment Fraud and Fairer Financial Services, described Andriesz's death as a "profound and preventable tragedy".

He said whistleblowers were "an essential part of the financial regulatory system" and warned there would be consequences for the integrity of the system if people did not believe they would be "treated properly, protected appropriately and listened to seriously".

The group of MPs called for the FCA to pay for an independent party to evaluate its handling of whistleblowers.

'Extreme retaliation and devastation'

In July, Andriesz told MPs and campaigners the FCA had been fully informed about other serious allegations he had made as long ago as 2018 and accused it of inaction.

The FCA told the BBC in July it had acted on his allegations and pointed to a supervision order it had issued based on his information.

But in Andriesz's view that amounted to little more than a regulatory "slap on the wrist" and made it harder to make a claim for whistleblower retaliation against BGC at tribunal.

Later that month, he told a meeting of the campaign group the Transparency Task Force the FCA was not fulfilling its obligations to the public and whistleblowers and merely "pays lip service" to the rules and regulations.

"It protects the institution and then exposes the whistleblower to extreme retaliation and devastation to their lives and families," he said.

The FCA told the BBC it was appointing a new non-executive director on its board, former Bank of England director Lea Paterson, to conduct a review into Andriesz's treatment and the FCA's handling of his whistleblower allegations.

An FCA spokesperson said: "We are very sorry to hear of Mr Andriesz's death. Our thoughts are with his family and friends.

"Since expressing our condolences, we'd asked Lea Paterson, who has just joined our board as a non-executive director, to review how we interacted with Mr Andriesz to learn any lessons for the future."

Jeremy Clarkson: Farming this year was 'an absolute disaster'

Published 5 October 2026

Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.

The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle by rising costs, but he was optimistic about the future.

He was greeted by loud applause from the Tory faithful, but joked that "a lot of people have come dressed as seats, I notice, around the edges there".

In a question and answer session alongside land agent Charlie Ireland, he also criticised the economic conditions faced by business owners, asking: "Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?"

Clarkson - who also hosts ITV's Who Wants to be a Millionaire - was introduced to the stage by the Conservative shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins.

Asked what kind of year he had had on the farm, Clarkson said: "We worked really hard all year and we ended up with, I think I'm right in saying, three ounces of hen food.

"It was an absolute disaster on the farming side but, I mean, luckily we've got other projects going on now.

"But the farming is very, very difficult – very, very difficult at the moment."

He added: "I'm very fortunate that I do have other income streams and newspaper columns, but if you're an ordinary farmer, it's not just the weather.

"Remember, it's as Charlie was saying, the attacks come from everywhere – whether it's Iran or Ukraine or taxes or energy costs – whatever it might be, it's just relentless."

The TV presenter has long been a Conservative supporter and was involved in the campaign against the Labour government's inheritance tax plans for farmers .

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government would levy inheritance tax on family farms in the party's first budget.

But the plan was watered down last year following the farmers' campaign and pressure from some of Labour's rural MPs.

Responding to Clarkson's comments, a government source said: "We are working with farmers to strengthen domestic food production and make supply chains more resilient as we build a stronger and more profitable farming sector together."

Clarkson also joked about comments by Labour MP Jenny Riddell-Carpenter who said the Britain of country pubs and black Labradors was a "nostalgic" false memory.

He joked that he was a "socialist" because he drinks lager and has two fox red Labradors, after it was reported Riddell-Carpenter told a Labour conference fringe event she feared the far right deciding what the vision of rural areas is.

Riddell-Carpenter had said: "It'll be that warm ale, a black Labrador by your feet in a pub that doesn't exist, and with symbolism of fox hunting all around them. It'll be a very far-right nostalgic vision of Britain that we don't want to have, (that) never really existed."

O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them"

Published 5 October 2026

First Minister Michelle O'Neill has dismissed a call from the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) to resign over her role in protests against the Drumcree parade.

The Sinn Féin vice-president was branded the "first minister of lawlessness" as unionists criticised the demonstrations on Garvaghy Road.

Police are investigating the unlawful protests which blocked an Orange Order march from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

Facing questions in the Stormont assembly, O'Neill said she was "proud" to stand with the residents and "will continue to stand with them".

She described the planned Orange march on 27 September as "unwanted, sectarian and triumphalist".

O'Neill was speaking on Monday in response to an urgent question on the Drumcree dispute tabled by DUP assembly member Phillip Brett.

O'Neill returns to Garvaghy Road as police investigate Sunday's 'unlawful protest' Published 5 days ago

Court of Appeal reserves judgement over Drumcree parade dispute Published 16 hours ago

An uneasy peace – how a week of the Drumcree parade dispute has unfolded Published 3 days ago

Michelle O'Neill was speaking in response to an urgent question from DUP MLA Phillip Brett

He called on O'Neill to "drop the bravado" and claimed she had shown "utter contempt" for the ministerial pledge of office.

Brett continued: "If you have been found to breach the ministerial code or the law, will you do the decent thing for once and resign as first minister?"

The first minister responded: "Catch yourself on, would be where I would start with that one.

"I'm going to continue to turn up for the people of the Garvaghy Road.

"I'm proud to stand with them and I will continue to stand with them."

Traditional Unionist Voice (TUV) assembly member Timothy Gaston accused O'Neill of being the "first minister of lawlessness" over her role in the street protests.

O'Neill replied: "I am the first minister of what is right."

She added that "we won't need to AI it" - a reference to a TUV councillor who posted online an AI image which exaggerated the size of a loyalist rally in Portadown.

DUP assembly member Jonathan Buckley questioned whether O'Neill would "accept and abide by the lawful decision of the courts" when appeal court judges make a ruling on the parade dispute.

Protesters along the Garvaghy Road, with the road blocked at a number of points on 27 September

The first minister said that "when the law is wrong I will stand firmly against it" and described the planned march as "morally wrong".

O'Neill later said "shame on you" to DUP assembly members over the party's handling of the Drumcree dispute.

"Your party has championed this," she said to DUP members on the opposite benches.

O'Neill flatly rejected a claim from Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) leader Jon Burrows that many people now regarded the first minister as "completely morally bankrupt".

Earlier, Stormont Speaker Edwin Poots raised concerns over the first minister not attending the chamber last week to answer the tabled urgent question.

The DUP assembly member said O'Neill's absence last Monday was "discourteous" to the assembly and the public.

"Members know my views on ministers being accountable to this house on behalf of the people who put us all here," he said.

stories.title: Shadow chancellor vows to cut at least one tax in every Tory budget
stories.summary: Shadow ministers unveiled a series of policies on day two of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 October 2026

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said he hopes to scrap at least one tax every budget if the Conservatives return to power, with the so-called "mansion tax" in his sights.

Speaking at the party's conference in Birmingham, Griffith said "lower, simpler and fairer taxes" would be his "personal north star" although he noted his ambition for cuts would take place "only when we can afford to do so".

He also said he would scrap the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), which takes effect from 2028 and introduces an extra levy for owners of properties in England valued at more than £2m.

Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government between 2010 and 2024.

Speaking on the main stage, Griffith said: "No country in history has ever taxed its way to prosperity, so we will cut taxes, but only when we can afford to do so, and always saying clearly how we will fund that within our golden economic rule."

The party's "golden economic rule" involves at least half of all savings identified going towards "deficit reduction, with the other half going to tax cuts and pro-growth measures".

Griffith likened his approach to that of former Tory Chancellor Nigel Lawson, adding: "It's my ambition to scrap at least one tax every budget. What would we prioritise? There's a lot.

"Tax cuts that help growth, tax cuts that improve incentives to work, tax cuts that make life simpler and fairer."

The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would be scrapped by the Conservatives.

Griffith sought to signal a different approach under Kemi Badenoch's leadership, telling members that the EPR was the "sort of thing the old Conservative Party went along with".

He also said Labour plans a "vindicative raid on family homes" in the form of the HVCTS, also dubbed the "mansion tax", which he would seek to scrap.

The shadow chancellor said: "It's an anti-growth tax that will distort the housing market and remove the incentive to make home improvements."

Ahead of his speech, Griffith was pressed on BBC Breakfast on whether he would keep the pensions triple lock, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham has proposed changing.

Griffith said: "We are going to keep it."

In 2021, then-backbencher Griffith wrote an article saying that the state pension triple lock was "unfair" as pensioners could "gain from the misfortune of others".

Senior Conservatives including former chancellor Jeremy Hunt and shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat have individually suggested the current triple lock is unsustainable.

Properties worth more than £2m in England face mansion tax Published 3 December 2025

Tories committed to pension triple lock, deputy leader says Published 4 days ago

Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow Published 27 September

During a series of speeches on Monday, Griffith and other shadow ministers also announced further details on the policies they believe will help free up businesses and grow the economy.

The proposals included ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, such as the future homes standard.

Griffith said the next Conservative government would support a third runway at Heathrow Airport. Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.

The Conservatives also want to implement a single levy for developers in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.

The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

Prospect general secretary Mike Clancy, whose union represents members in Natural England and the Environment Agency, said: "Conservative budget cuts have left these regulators struggling to perform their vital functions with 'lack of resources' the most common reason for planning delays.

"The solution is to restore their funding to adequate levels, not scrap vital safeguards."

'Fantasy-land' pledges

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth, anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.

She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn."

Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies".

He added the Tories were unable to match Reform's pledge to raise the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 .

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said scrapping rules that "secure affordable homes and vital community infrastructure is not a plan for growth".

She added: "It is a gift to developers, leaving communities to pick up the bill for new housing while handing ordinary people higher costs and fewer protections."

stories.title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
stories.summary: US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The US has withdrawn all of its bombers from RAF Fairford

Published 5 October 2026

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base.

The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.

US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

A No 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

Peace for villagers as US bombers leave UK airbase Published 23 hours ago

What makes RAF Fairford one of the UK's most important military sites? Published 7 days ago

He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world".

Speaking on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not directly tie last week's incident to the decision to pull bombers from RAF Fairford.

He added: "It's not unusual to see movement of assets to different parts of the world based on exercises, redeployments, people changing out and new people coming in, new planes coming in and old planes going out."

Rubio said the US still has full confidence in the security of all its bases and that British authorities have been very cooperative since the incident.

US Vice President JD Vance later said the bombers were moved out of an "abundance of caution", adding Washington feels Iran is doing what it has "done for 49 years... which is engage in acts of terrorism against the US and against a lot of other people".

RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.

Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.

Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.

The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.

Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.

The newspaper wrote that the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.

Ezra Cohen, who served as a defence official under Trump's first administration, called the US' decision "prudent".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "These are very, very unique platforms that aren't being produced anymore, and we have a limited number of them. The B-1 bomber is a strategic asset, and we're going to take steps to protect it from all sorts of threats."

It is technically possible for the US to conduct precision strikes directly from the US without a UK base - like in Operation Midnight Hammer last year .

But the removal of the bombers from RAF Fairford will see the US lose a foothold for the country outside continental Europe.

Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called the US' decision to withdraw its bombers "deeply concerning" and called for the government to set out a plan to ensure the country's military bases are "fit for purpose".

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.

Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.

In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

Residents living close to RAF Fairford told the BBC of their relief at the departure of bombers from the airbase, with one local saying she was "thrilled," citing the noise and feeling "increasingly vulnerable" in recent weeks.

Another villager, who said he has seen bombs being loaded aboard aircraft from his back garden, said he knew something was happening when he saw planes leaving "one, after another, after another" on Sunday.

stories.title: Would the Conservatives' plan make new houses £50,000 cheaper?
stories.summary: BBC Verify looks into the shadow chancellor's plan to cut some building regulations to reduce construction costs.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 October 2026

Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has said his party, if it was returned to power, would take £50,000 off the cost of building a new home in England and Wales by cutting back on regulations.

The £50,000 figure claimed by Griffith reflects estimates by the housebuilding industry of the costs of new regulations and taxes.

However, construction and housing experts warn that some of the savings could ultimately lead to higher government spending on schools, roads, and affordable housing.

And some analysts also warn the Conservative plans to scrap environmental regulations could potentially push up household energy bills in future.

Where does the £50,000 figure come from?

The Conservatives argue a number of regulations are adding to the cost of constructing and delivering new private homes.

These include:

The Community Infrastructure Levy - a charge on certain new developments in England and Wales which councils can use to fund local infrastructure such as roads, schools and play areas

The Future Homes Standard which requires new-build homes in England to meet higher energy-efficiency standards and use low-carbon heating such as heat pumps rather than gas boilers

Section 106 which can require developers to provide a proportion of social or affordable housing in England as part of a new development.

The Tories say they will scrap or reform these and other regulations, saying: "All in all, we will cut the cost of delivering and therefore buying a new home by up to £50,000."

BBC Verify has asked the Conservatives for a full breakdown of their figure.

What does the construction industry say?

The Home Builders Federation (HBF) has estimated that new regulations, taxes and inflation - since 2020 - have increased the cost of building an individual new home in England and Wales by £76,000.

It says this represents around 20% of the value of an average new home.

Of this total, it estimates:

£985 comes from Section 106

£10,200 comes from the Future Homes Standard

£12,700 in environmental protection measures such as "nutrient neutrality" and "biodiversity net gain"

Excluding a £37,000 increase in the costs of material and labour, the HBF estimates that regulations and taxes have added around £42,000 to the cost of building a new home.

The Conservatives' estimate is slightly higher than the HBF's figure. The HBF also includes nearly £8,000 to reflect changes in building regulations. The Conservatives have not said they would find savings by scrapping all of those.

The party's plan also assumes the savings they have highlighted would be passed on to buyers rather than raising house builders' profits.

Could these savings be achieved?

Noble Francis of trade body the Construction Products Association (CPA) told BBC Verify that new costs imposed on builders through regulations and taxes in recent years - including the time firms spend navigating the regulatory system - are a serious constraint on residential construction rates.

The Labour government is well off track in terms of meeting its target of building 1.5 million net additional dwellings in England over the course of this parliament - which requires an annual building rate of around 300,000 homes per year.

In the year to June only around 203,000 were built, according to official estimates.

However, Francis also said: "It's easy for any party not in government to just claim they will get rid of red tape and cut costs but both the Conservatives and Labour have been in power in the last five years and have added extra costs to house building."

The Future Homes Standard, for instance, was first proposed in 2019 when Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson was in power.

Other analysts point out that the upfront construction cost savings from the plan could potentially lead to higher government spending in the future.

Housing expert Anna Clarke said: "Cutting the costs of house building by £50,000 would be really helpful in getting much-needed new homes built.

"But if you don't get developers to pay for new schools and infrastructure you need to pay for them some other way."

And some analysts argue that updated environmental building standards, such as requiring heat pumps rather than gas boilers in new homes, are forecast to save households money in the long-term by reducing their domestic energy bills.

Dr Richard Lowes of clean energy advocates the Regulatory Assistance Project told BBC Verify: "If the energy bill implications are not carefully considered, households may be lumbered with very high bills for decades.

"The lowest running costs can typically be achieved with heat pumps paired with solar and batteries."

Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett and Daniel Wainwright

stories.title: Ex-Manchester leader defends deals with Man City owners
stories.summary: Veteran former council leader Sir Richard Leese says the relationship has been beneficial to the city.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sir Richard Leese was leader of Manchester City Council for 25 years before he stepped down in 2021

Published 5 October 2026

The former leader of Manchester City Council has defended the council's relationship with the owners of Manchester City amid questions over land deals.

Sir Richard Leese, who was head of the council for 25 years until 2021 and is also honorary president of the club, said a decade-old deal with Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) was "good for the city".

The partnership between the authority and the company owned by Sheik Mansour bin zayed Al Nahyan has come under renewed scrutiny since City was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations with "sham" commercial contracts .

The club has denied any wrongdoing is appealing against the charges.

The council entered into a partnership with ADUG in 2014 when they formed a joint venture called Manchester Life.

It planned to invest more than £1bn over the next decade and develop thousands of homes in the Ancoats and New Islington areas, on the edge of the city centre close to the club's Etihad stadium.

But in 2022, a report by the University of Sheffield, called Manchester Offshored, raised questions about the wider public value of the schemes, and a lack of transparency around their finances.

It highlighted the absence of any affordable housing in the projects, and that the joint venture companies were ultimately owned by ADUG through firms registered offshore.

Abu Dhabi United Group are majority shareholders in City Football Group - which owns Manchester City FC

A deal struck in 2015 saw ADUG effectively given the first pick of land in Ancoats and New Islington. The University of Sheffield report argued that land was leased to ADUG at "below comparable rates".

Sir Richard said the 2015 deal was "brokered by the UK government with the UAE government".

"It was a time when development in Manchester had stopped," he said.

"We were still suffering from the 2008 crash, from the recession that followed that.

"There was criticism at the time though - and there still is now - that the land was given away too cheaply by the city council.

"The point is, the investment from Abu Dhabi is what created the value.

"That deal allowed development to be kick-started - particularly in the Ancoats area.

"All of this was documented and went through reports that went through the council's due processes.

"I think it has been demonstrated that the deal was a good deal and a good deal for Manchester."

'Real credibility'

Abu Dhabi's investment in Manchester City started in 2008, when City Football Group – majority-owned by ADUG - bought the club in a £200m deal.

With significant investment from its new owners, the club went on to win its first trophy in 36 years with an FA Cup win in 2011 and a dramatic Premier League title followed the next year.

The club went on to win the league seven more times between 2013 and 2024.

But the Premier League began investigating the club's financial dealings in 2018, and City was charged in 2023.

Last week, it was announced the club had been found guilty of 115 charges, including some around a so-called disguised funding scheme, which was said to have seen the club's owners topping up sponsorship and commercial deals with their own funding running to more than £800m.

Andy Burnham has said Manchester City's owners had been a "huge partner" in Manchester

When asked last week about potential fallout from the City charges, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was metropolitan mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 to 2026, said he would be "really concerned" if the owners were to pull out of the club.

He added: "They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is."

Since then, it has been reported that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) may halt UK-wide investment schemes worth billions of pounds as a result of the Premier League ruling.

Sir Richard said he hoped that Manchester did not lose UEA investment, adding: "I think certainly Abu Dhabi will be thinking that they have been very badly treated given the contribution that they have made - not just to Manchester but to English football as well."

He added: "I would be concerned if they did stop investing. I don't think they'd give us up."

Sir Richard told BBC Radio 4's Today programme earlier that "the investment in Manchester from Abu Dhabi has been very significant".

Stressing he was not speaking on behalf of the club, he pointed to the investment in City, its training complex and the City Football Group headquarters.

He added: "I think for the city, one thing about working with Abu Dhabi is everything that they promised they have delivered.

"So they have real credibility in the city. That's something we'd want to maintain.

"I don't think any other football club has got anywhere near the sort of contribution that they have made to their local community.

"What has been created in Manchester City is a phenomenon really and that has to be maintained in some way whatever the final outcome of the allegations against them."

'Achieved'

Manchester City Council also defended the benefits of the partnership with Manchester Life as a "platform for future development".

"The claim that working in partnership with Manchester City's owners has not been a good deal for the council or the city has been debunked repeatedly," the authority said.

"Claims that some land was sold too cheaply to Manchester Life ignore the fact that there was zero market interest at the time of the sale, that the land is worth more now precisely because of Manchester Life's investment and the significant financial return the council is receiving through profit-sharing arrangements.

"Manchester Life was always envisaged as a platform for further investment. Its success should be measured in what it has delivered directly and what it has unlocked.

"The partnership was set up to deliver significant housing development, create an investor confidence and a platform for other developers to come into the market and invest in Manchester - which it has achieved."

stories.title: Tensions exposed among Greens by 'Zionism is racism' conference vote
stories.summary: What may be troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 October 2026

It is not exactly typical for a British party conference, let alone that of one of the smaller parties, to elicit international condemnation.

Yet that is the position the Green Party of England and Wales is in today after Israel's foreign ministry said it was banning their leader, Zack Polanski, from entering the country.

The cause was the motion proposed by party members and adopted by the conference on Sunday, declaring Zionism, which is the belief in the right to a Jewish homeland, to be racism.

The Green motion describes Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", and supports instead a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

It's hardly likely that Polanski or indeed many Greens are going to be much troubled by Israel's condemnation of the motion. One major factor in the Greens' electoral gains over the past year or so, a hugely successful period for the party, has been their clear and vocal condemnation of Israel's war in Gaza and actions in the region more generally.

What may be more troubling for the Greens institutionally is what this episode reveals about some of the dynamics in the party.

Many Greens are proud of the party's internal democracy: this motion was proposed by and voted on by party members. Yet that has resulted in the scenario of leading Green elected politicians facing scrutiny over party policy which the vast majority of them opposed.

Polanski, who is not an MP, wanted changes to the motion which were rejected by the conference, and ultimately did not participate in the debate or vote. Of the Greens' five MPs, four opposed the motion.

The most vocal of them was Adrian Ramsay, the MP for Waveney Valley, who was a Green co-leader for four years until September last year when he and his running mate were defeated by Polanski by a vast margin.

Polanski banned from Israel after party's motion declaring 'Zionism is racism' Published 1 day ago

Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion Published 23 hours ago

So an element of this is the changing nature of the Greens' activist base under Polanski's leadership, moving away from an environmental focus to a more general left-populist politics, incorporating a large element of 'anti-imperialist' foreign policy.

Yet this may not be the last issue where that results in a public dispute between the membership and their MPs, four of whom were elected at the last general election under different leadership.

And it is striking that, though Polanski's election as leader was a clear symbol of that shift in the Greens' approach, he did not back this motion. So this could presage tensions too between Polanski and the party membership, some of whom will have been inspired to join the Greens by his leadership.

In practical terms, the Green MPs will be able to continue espousing a different position in parliament to the party's new policy.

The Greens do not have a whipping system, meaning that MPs are free to vote as they wish. This is also true of their councillors, including in the almost 40 councils where the Greens are in power after the May local elections.

It will be interesting to see whether as a result of these tensions there is a push either to constrain the ability of the party conference to make policy, or in the other direction - to constrain the ability of elected representatives to defy party policy.

Electoral reform

Separately, this motion may present a political headache down the line for Andy Burnham.

In his Labour conference speech last week, the prime minister said he was forming a "national commission" on electoral reform, with a view to changing the system used for general elections in the long-term.

While Burnham did not specify what system he wanted, he said that Labour would at the next general election commit to a new system where "everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard".

Under a move to any more proportional system, on current trends, there would likely be more Green MPs as a result. In the scenario of a hung parliament, the Greens are a party to which Labour would naturally look for support as part of the progressive bloc.

And yet the Greens are also now a party whose actions this weekend have been condemned by the Labour chair, Bridget Phillipson, as "shameful" and "fundamentally wrong". Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, said the Zionism motion "crosses a line and is rightly being condemned across the political spectrum."

Labour has long been divided on the question of electoral reform. Their leader now has a clear position in favour but the Green motion this weekend could have the unintended effect of bolstering opposition within Labour to that element of the prime minister's agenda.

Bottles of water and sweets poking fun at Andy Burnham were handed out at the Conservative Party conference

Published 5 October 2026

An artist has said he is taking legal advice after accusing the Conservative Party of copying his portrait of Andy Burnham at their party conference.

People attending the event in Birmingham have been handed water bottles featuring the image and labelled "Bottler Burnham" and "0% strength" and sweets labelled "Andy Panders' People Pleaser Pick N Mix".

Labour supporter Stanley Chow, who created the image for Burnham's 2021 mayoral campaign in Greater Manchester, has claimed the party did not ask for permission to use the image.

A Conservative Party spokeswoman said the bottles were not on sale and merely handed out to attending media in "goody bags".

Manchester illustrator Chow said: "I was stunned and angry when I saw what they had done. It is childish from them. I am taking legal advice.

"I'm very disappointed. It's frustrating that an institution like the Conservative Party has no idea that they are infringing copyright."

The original image of Andy Burnham was created by Chow in 2021

The artist claimed Reform UK had also infringed his copyright by using the image a few months ago in AI-generated social media campaign posts.

A Reform UK spokesman said at the time that it had "removed the posts in good faith and without any admission of liability on our part".
