stories.title: Jewish Greens chair says she could leave party over 'Zionism is racism' motion
stories.summary: The motion, which has divided senior party figures, backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein said the motion "crosses a line"

Published 5 October 2026

The chair of Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein has told the BBC it is "quite possible" she will leave the party after Green members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.

The motion, which has divided senior party figures, also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It has been condemned by some Jewish groups and Israel's foreign ministry.

Asked by BBC Radio 4's Today programme about her future, Lichtenstein said: "I haven't decided yet...It is quite possible that I will leave the party...I'm giving it a little time and to talk with colleagues."

Lichtenstein, who is a former chair of her local party, said she had opposed the motion from the first time she heard about it.

"I don't think it's helpful and it doesn't make any difference whatsoever to Palestinians in Gaza who have suffered devastation, orphans left behind, it doesn't make any difference to Palestinians in the West Bank who are currently suffering, are currently being attacked and killed."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The party's leader Zack Polanski, who is himself Jewish, had called for the motion to be amended to add in protections for Jewish members and remove language referring to a "single democratic Palestinian State". Both of these amendments were defeated.

Polanski did not stay at conference to vote on either this or the substantive motion. He left early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here .

The motion, among other statements, "supports the establishment of a single democratic Palestinian State in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital, equal rights for all, and the right of return for Palestinians and their descendants".

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it".

Lichtenstein said she defines herself as "both Zionist and anti-Zionist" depending on the definition, and said a problem with the motion is that there are many definitions.

She said she was not concerned about "people accusing me of supporting Israel's right to exist and therefore I'm a racist, which of course is not the case", but said the "very bad motion...crosses a line".

One way in which it did that, she said, was that the proposers said they had consulted some Jews, but did not consult the Jewish Greens, who would have made some amendments to improve the motion.

She said there was a "vast range" of opinions among Jewish Greens, some who supported the motion entirely, others who supported aspects, and others who were against it. Some Jewish Greens also support one state, she added.

She said that party policy was that "it's up to Israelis and Palestinians to choose their future - one state or two".

Last month, the UK and 11 allies reiterated their support for a two-state solution , which would recognise a Palestinian state alongside an Israeli one. Israel rejects a two-state solution.

Her concern with the motion was that the Green Party may accuse UK, Israeli, or Jewish organisations, including those that partner with Palestinians, of racism. She said she supports many of these groups working "against the occupation and even go out on the ground to assist Palestinians".

She said she knows of some non-Jews who are planning on not staying in the party because "they think the motion crosses a line" and also because of their work, if they might not be able to be associated with a party that has "Zionism is racism" as a policy.

Asked whether she believed there were antisemites inside the party, including at senior levels, she said "there are certainly some antisemites in the party, I don't know about at senior level, that is not my experience".

The motion was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813

In response to the motion, Israel's foreign ministry said it had banned Polanski from entering the country.

A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.

Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

"We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added.

Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay, Carla Denyer, and Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, but the leadership was divided.

In her interview on the Today programme on Friday, co-deputy leader Rachel Millward had called the motion "problematic", while her counterpart Mothin Ali told the BBC on Saturday he would support the motion in its original form.

The Movement for Progressive Judaism, one of the largest and most liberal strands of Judaism in the UK, released a statement condemning the motion, which it said was "antisemitic in its formulation and intention".

"Jewish self-determination is a right. Declaring it racist is an attack on Jews," the statement read.

Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis also called the motion "poisonous antisemitism, a threat to British Jews and to Britain".

The Green Party motion said it "rejects attempts" to - among other things - "equate anti-Zionism with antisemitism" and said "we affirm that definitions of anti-Jewish discrimination should not equate Jewish identity with Zionist ideology or political practice".

Opposition parties pushed back against the motion.

Labour chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards".

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp criticised the motion on behalf of the Conservatives, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core".

Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the "divisive" motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK.

stories.title: 'Don't axe Youth Parliament' pleads teen member
stories.summary: The government plans to no longer fund the scheme launched to get young people into politics.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Aman Fatima has been a Member of Youth Parliament for two years

Published 5 October 2026

A taxpayer-funded programme aimed at boosting young people's interest in politics should not be axed just because "money is tight", one of its members has said.

Last month the BBC learned the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) would not be committing to giving any more grants to the UK Youth Parliament.

"If the government is to cut the Youth Parliament there should be reasons and there has to be alternatives, even if the funding is tight," Aman Fatima, MYP for Essex, told BBC Politics East.

The government said it was working on a new scheme to increase young people's involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements due this autumn.

Established in 1999, the parliament takes place at the House of Commons and boasts more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18, including Aman.

She said if the scheme – run by the National Youth Agency – was scrapped, an alternative must be found because "young people are the next generation" of government.

"Money is tight but you also want young people's opinions; them to tell you what's wrong and the challenges they are facing," she said.

"And the [Youth Parliament] really helps young people get their voice out there, especially in a big place such as the House of Commons."

Members of the UK Youth Parliament, formed in 1999, hold an annual debate within in the House of Commons every year

As part of the programme, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting, once a year.

In recent years, they have campaigned on issues such as votes for 16-year-olds and for free period products to be made available to students.

"There are lots of opinions from people saying that they haven't seen any difference made, but I think we do contribute to how the government works today," added Aman.

In the last year, the youth parliament received £453,000 in taxpayer funding with about £2.4m public money spent on it between 2017 and 2024.

No final decision has been made on funding after March 2027, but a government source said Downing Street would no longer commit to it "in its current form."

Labour MP Jess Asato believes there are other ways for young people to make their mark in politics

Jess Asato, Labour MP for Lowestoft, said she believed the decision had been made because the Youth Parliament was not producing "a diversity of voices".

"I think what the government's trying to say is we need things much more locally that bring a lot more young people into that political or democratic engagement," she said.

"In East Suffolk we have a fantastic youth council and that means lots and lots more young people can get involved in things that they care about locally.

"But I do wish the government might look at this [decision] again."

Conservative MP Patrick Spencer said funding for Labour government's plans had to come from somewhere

Patrick Spencer, Conservative MP for Central Suffolk and North Ipswich, said: "The reality is this government needs to make cuts because it needs to fund things that it's planning to do.

"It's one of the difficult decisions that has got to be made."

The DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy" and said it had given elected young people "a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work".

stories.body:
Trump supporters may be surprised to learn the state takeover of means of production is not driven by the left

Americans will never accept the Democratic party’s slide to the left, or so desperate Republicans are hoping.

With the midterm elections fast upon us, Zohran Mamdani’s promise of a few city-run bodegas in New York City will scare the bejeezus out of middle America. Disgust over the democratic socialists’ unicorn-and-puppy promises of a world without capitalism will keep the Republicans in power.

Leading the charge against the new reds-under-the-bed is Donald Trump. “Together, we will defeat communism,” Trump promised in his recent TV ads .

Trump’s supporters might be surprised to discover that the United States is, indeed, sliding in the direction of a command and control economy. But the state takeover of the means of production is not being driven by the left. The grab for the US’s productive resources is the project of none other than Trump – who, it’s a fair guess, has never read Lenin.

The latest evidence comes in data crunched by the V-Dem project in Sweden, which measures the erosion of democracy around the world. It built a scale to gauge “state ownership of the economy”. As noted by Cullen Hendrix from the Peterson Institute for International Economics, from 2002 to 2024, the US ranked among the four countries with the least state control. In 2025, the first year of Trump’s second term, it dropped from second place to 16th.

By November of last year, the Trump administration had spent more than $10bn taking stakes in companies he deemed essential for national security, from Intel to a range of ventures mining for critical minerals. It also acquired an option to take a stake in Westinghouse, which makes nuclear reactors. And it blackmailed Nippon Steel into granting Trump’s Washington a “golden share” in exchange for the go-ahead to purchase US Steel.

To be fair, Trump’s acquisitiveness notwithstanding, the US is not even close to flirting with the flavor of socialism favored by the Soviet Union and its satellites in the second half of the 20th century. By the V-Dem accounting, Washington’s stake in the economy is still smaller than in 163 countries.

Government-run companies are a standard feature in many market economies. The Norwegian government has a majority stake in its massive oil company, which puts the country in 18th place. Even “communist” countries are pretty capitalist: private companies contribute 60% of China’s GDP .

And in a geopolitical landscape shaped by competition with China, there is a reasonable case to be made for Washington to take equity stakes in industries that are critical for American leadership and security, and which might not develop autonomously in competition with rivals heavily subsidized by Beijing.

Yet Trump’s wanton lunge for private assets lacks the discipline required for this kind of strategic positioning.

The president’s statist leanings mark a dramatic break with the market-focused presidencies of his recent predecessors, Democrat and Republican. The question is, what motivates him? His appetites are embedded in a body of thought that is skeptical, if not outright hostile, towards essential building blocks of the global market economy. He has pushed back against globalization since his first term in office, seemingly drawn to the Marxist-inspired dependency theory , which washed across Latin America in the 1960s and 1970s proposing protectionism and state industrial policy as a path to economic development.

His lust to control the economy is there for all to see. Though the supreme court already slapped down his attempt to take over trade policy from Congress, he is still threatening to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT”. His promise to give $5,000 to every American if Republicans maintain control of Congress in November’s elections underscores how he views the state’s coffers as his private piggy bank. Even his commie-bashing ads were paid for by taxpayer dollars.

Still, he clearly has no interest in the dictatorship of the proletariat, caring little if at all for the fate of the downtrodden. His preferred flavor of redistribution takes from those on the bottom to give to those on the top.

If anything, Trump reminds us that socialism is not the only ideological justification for state projects to take control over resources and wealth.

Watching the US president bow to Xi Jinping last week, it’s tempting to think that Trump wants to emulate China’s leader. Xi gets to rule unimpeded over more than one billion Chinese. He gets to shape China’s society and economy at will – purging this rival, raising that sycophant to power.

But Xi’s China is too disciplined for Trump. The Chinese leader still relies on hordes of technocrats to execute a coherent strategy aimed to achieve technological superiority. The US president doesn’t have the attention span for this kind of thing.

Rather, Trump’s model might be Vladimir Putin, who rules Russia like a fiefdom. Or maybe one of those dictators the US used to support in Latin America during the cold war: Haiti’s Papa Doc Duvalier or Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who saw government as a tool to enrich their families and cement dynasties in power. If nothing else, Trump’s dealings with crypto suggest he views his administration as a road to family riches.

Karl Marx may not be Trump’s guiding light. But his writings can help understand Trump’s place in history. Marx proposes that his tome The 18th Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, about the 1851 coup that brought Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte to power in France, was meant to “demonstrate how the class struggle in France created circumstances and relationships that made it possible for a grotesque mediocrity to play a hero’s part”.

Americans may be grateful that their most recent class struggles didn’t produce a homegrown Lenin. But they did deliver Donald Trump .

Perhaps this does not condemn the US to an autocratic future. Hendrix points out that while Trump “clearly wants to be king”, the US’s political economy may not let him. Putin managed to establish autocratic rule over a fairly primitive, oil-based economy. This kind of control “is much harder to achieve in a modern complex economy” such as that of the United States, Hendrix noted. You can’t simply seize the oil to run the place.

Though Trump may fail, Americans’ acquiescence as he grabs for power raises a question for those who freak out over Mamdani’s city-run bodegas: why is Trump’s lurch to take over the American economy any better than what they hear from the Democratic Socialists of America?

stories.title: ASOS app users receive push notifications apparently sent by hackers
stories.summary: Dozens of people appear to have received a strange message from the clothing and beauty store's app.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 6 October 2026, 10:49 BST

Asos users across the UK have been sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company.

Dozens of people have told the BBC about receiving a strange message from the clothing and beauty store's app, appearing on their phone screens.

"Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message reads.

Asos did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for comment.

"If confirmed, this is a deeply serious attack because the hackers appear to have done something particularly brazen: turned ASOS's own app into their ransom note," says Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point.

"Millions of people trust notifications from apps on their phones because they are supposed to come directly from the company."

Extortion message

On social media, dozens of people have posted about receiving the message - confused as to what it means.

Although the apparent extortion message has been issued directly to customers, it is addressed to Asos' data protection officer (DPO) and IT team.

The message claims the unnamed hackers have "fully compromised the Snowflake instance".

This refers to the data storage company Snowflake, whose tools are used by dozens of firms for collecting, analysing and storing data.

It is not known if ASOS is a customer of Snowflake or what data, if any, is stored with the service.

But Snowflake has been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years and has been linked to incidents targeting services including Ticketmaster and Santander .

It is, however, very unusual for a data breach to be revealed quite so publicly - and for customers to be informed in this manner.

Most extortions and negotiations by cyber criminals are conducted in private, with hackers hoping their discretion will result in a quiet pay-off.

The pop up message contains a link to the hackers' Telegram channel.

The new group is calling itself Xuanye Group and only created it's Telegram channel today.

They have posted only three times with the latest being about the ASOS hack.

Dan Bird, from cyber security firm Horizon3 says the pop up message the criminals sent implies that their access has gone beyond the Snowflake database.

"Sending a push notification to ASOS's app users would require access to the company's notification system, which is separate from the Snowflake data platform the attackers claim to have compromised."

"If both claims hold up, it suggests the attackers got hold of credentials that opened more than one door," he said.

stories.title: Lego fraudster among last year's most high-profile insurance scammers
stories.summary: The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, the insurance trade body, the ABI said.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 hours ago

A scammer jailed for making false home insurance claims about supposedly stolen Lego has been listed as one of last year's most high-profile insurance fraudsters.

The person was sentenced to 28 months in prison after an investigation found the claims were made up, insurance trade body the ABI said.

Other insurance fraud cases flagged by the ABI include someone who staged car crashes with people they met online and a complex travel insurance scam involving multiple fake identities and documents.

The average value of a fraudulent claim reached £14,300 last year, the second-highest level on record, the ABI said.

There was £1.34bn worth of fraudulent claims in 2025, a 14% increase on the £1.18bn detected the previous year.

At the same time, the number of detected fraudulent claims fell slightly to 93,900, down 2.7% on 2024.

Mark Allen, head of fraud and financial crime at the ABI, said: "Although the rate of detected insurance fraud fell slightly last year, our data shows that fraudsters are targeting much bigger payouts.

"As emerging technologies such as AI become more widely available, fraudsters will continue to look for new ways to exploit them."

Det Ch Insp Simon Klust, head of the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department (IFED) at the City of London Police, said: "Insurance fraud is not a victimless crime and those who commit it increase the cost of premiums for honest customers."

He added that the 250 cases a day detected by the ABI last year were "unfortunately likely to be just the tip of the iceberg".

Macbooks, fishing equipment and Lego sets

One of the most notable fraudsters identified by the ABI last year was a man found by IFED to have fabricated reports of stolen high-value Lego sets , external .

The man's scam claims to Axa Insurance during 2021 and 2022 also included other high-value items such as MacBooks, televisions, gaming consoles and fishing equipment, IFED said.

In 2023, IFED said it found collectible Lego sets matching the ones claimed to have been stolen displayed in the man's living room during a search.

Alongside his prison sentence handed down last year, he was also ordered to repay the £14,000 he had claimed.

Other cases highlighted by the ABI included a man jailed for 20 months for manipulating women he met on dating sites into participating in staged car crashes, and a man sentenced to four and a half years for submitting over £300,000 worth of fraudulent travel medical emergency claims.

In general, the ABI said motor insurance remained the area where insurers identified the most fraudulent cases, accounting for 55% of all scam claims.

Meanwhile, the ABI's figures found that exaggerated loss remains the most common type of insurance fraud, with 26,900 cases identified.

This is when someone deliberately attempts to increase the cost of a claim beyond its true value, the ABI said.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures

Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe , as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.

The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely , and the EU imposes duties of up to 45% .

EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.

Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China .

Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models , and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant , from investing further in the UK.

“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.

“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”

Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.

Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.

Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.

The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”

.

Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”

after newsletter promotion

Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”

He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”

Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.

Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.

Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.

Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”

He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

stories.title: We're saving £100 a month for our kids but they won't get it until they're 57
stories.summary: Why a growing number of parents are opening pensions for their children.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices now

Published 6 October 2026, 00:00 BST

Richard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them.

The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules. , external

So the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083.

Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing.

"Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow."

'We don't eat out as often as we used to'

Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council.

He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended.

In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18.

The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life.

Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past.

"We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain.

"And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids."

'I want to retire earlier so this will help'

Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600.

The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show.

One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open , external as in the same period a year earlier.

Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023.

While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more?

Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years.

"The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help."

Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says.

Hugo Thompson is happy to wait until he is at least 57 to access the pension fund

For parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity.

"Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound."

It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children.

In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts.

Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half.

Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three.

Wally Luckeydoo says he is giving his children a "financial head start"

"My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally.

"For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt.

"I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially."

stories.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
stories.summary: Top executive Jason Kwon tells hearing company has added "more precautions" to its training environments.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney

Published 6 October 2026, 05:39 BST

OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.

"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.

Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.

When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.

"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.

"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."

Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.

"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.

The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.

Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.

This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.

The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".

"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.

"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.

The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.

"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.

Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

stories.title: Irish budget to tackle childcare and energy costs
stories.summary: The threshold at which people start paying the higher income tax rate is also expected to increase.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 5 hours ago

The Irish government is expected to announce measures to help with energy and childcare costs when it delivers its budget later.

The threshold at which people start paying the higher rate of income tax is also expected to be increased from its current level of €44,000 (£37,000).

The Taoiseach (Irish Prime Minister) Micheál Martin said the budget has to be about "trying to ease the pressure on families and households".

The broad shape of the budget was set out in the Summer Economic Statement , external , promising tax measures worth €1.5bn (£1.27bn) and extra spending of €7bn (£5.92bn).

Government party leaders, including the taoiseach, are expected to sign off on the budget

Much of that additional spending is "standstill" funding to cover the rising costs of current services.

Ireland is in a stronger fiscal position than most European countries as an ongoing corporation tax windfall means it is collecting more in taxes than it is spending on services.

Figures released last week showed the country is expected to run a surplus of €6.9bn (£5.84bn) this year, lower than the €9.2bn (£7.79bn) forecast in April.

That smaller forecast surplus reflects the introduction of fuel supports and additional spending to cover budget overspends, particularly in health.

Some of the surplus is being invested in national wealth funds to help with future spending commitments.

'Culture card' for teens

A spending watchdog, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, has criticised the government for not saving more.

Other measures expected to be announced on Tuesday are a new tax-free savings scheme, similar to the UK ISA.

A proposal for a "culture card" for teenagers, to spend on events like concerts, is also set to be announced though the value and eligibility are unclear.

stories.title: Last call for the mall? How shopping centres are reinventing themselves
stories.summary: In the internet age, medium-sized retail hubs are looking for new ways to survive and thrive.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Keith Ely remembers the Brunel Centre's heyday but is looking to the future

Published 5 hours ago

The Brunel Centre was once a thriving retail destination, attracting shoppers from far and wide.

"It was incredible," says town councillor Keith Ely, who remembers its opening in Bletchley, Buckinghamshire, in 1973.

Back then, centre:MK, a large destination shopping centre four miles away in Milton Keynes, did not exist, and the Brunel was quite the draw.

Now, like many other medium-sized shopping centres, it is struggling.

Vacant units and graffiti-daubed shutters dominate, and it has just one store left.

That remaining shop, a Boots Opticians, is set to close later this month ahead of the centre's planned demolition next year .

But Ely, 87, is not upset to see the Brunel make way for flats and a health centre, with only some retail space.

"It is a sad old building, isn't it?" he says. "There is no nostalgia from me."

The Debenhams store in the Grafton Centre in Cambridge closed in 2021

In the Grafton Centre, Cambridge, it is a similar story, with shuttered units, a large empty former Debenhams department store and a permanently closed cinema.

There are long-term plans for a redevelopment to include retail but also a life science centre.

This may work in Cambridge, a global leader in life sciences, but it is not an option in much of the country.

So, in the age of online shopping, what lies ahead for these medium-sized malls?

"There are too many in the UK and many don't have a future," is the stark assessment of Subjit Jassy, a director at Pioneer Group, which owns the centre.

"The old model of retailers expanding to improve turnover has now disappeared because of the internet."

Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, Before the Brunel Shopping Centre was built in the 1970s, people in Bletchley would travel to Aylesbury or Bedford to shop

Image source, Milton Keynes Living Archive Image caption, The centre initially had little natural light, before the roof was replaced with glass

Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, In 2021 Milton Keynes City Council was awarded £22.7m from the government's Town Deal Fund to redevelop the site

Image source, Qays Najm/BBC Image caption, Boots Opticians, the last remaining store in the centre, is already closed on Wednesdays

1 of 4

Analysis by commercial property firm CBRE , external found that while the vacancy rate across UK shopping centres in the second quarter of this year was 16%, it was "significantly lower" at major centres.

Meanwhile, research by estate agents Savills found between April and June 2026 almost 73% of consumer spending in shopping centres was in the biggest sites, with less than 18% in secondary, or medium-sized centres.

Dr Kardi Somerfield says centres that have leisure businesses can "extend the day" and attract customers into the evening

"It is not just that shopping centres have one destiny; they really don't," says Dr Kardi Somerfield, a lecturer in marketing at the University of Northampton.

Some destination shopping centres are running at "almost 100% occupancy", she adds.

Back at the Brunel, Labour's Ed Hume, responsible for housing at Milton Keynes City Council, says: "We do need shops.

"The change here is about making sure we have a town centre that is much more open."

The hope is that more town centre homes will increase the number of people to use local businesses.

Similar plans in Norwich will see the Anglia Square development primarily replaced by housing.

Characters from TV show The Flintstones were at the opening of the Weston Favell Shopping Centre in 1974

But there are other options rather than just tearing a centre down.

Market Walk in Northampton is t o become a leisure and entertainment space .

"Other shopping centres have a really important purpose as a community hub," says Somerfield, outlining another potential use.

This is what management are trying to achieve at another site that opened in the 1970s: Weston Favell, on the eastern edge of Northampton.

Footfall – the number of customers entering the building – has increased every year since the pandemic, says centre manager Kevin Legg.

"We are still relevant today," he says.

"Other shopping centres are trying to emulate and create what we've got."

What they have got is a mix of a large supermarket, a number of big national brands and smaller independent businesses, as well as other community facilities.

Not far from the library inside the centre is a church. It is currently being used by Silhouette Youth Theatre, a charity that aims to make the arts more accessible.

Next year it plans to create a 250-seat theatre inside part of a former Wilko store.

Silhouette Youth Theatre currently holds sessions in the Emmanuel Church, inside Weston Favell Shopping Centre

George Grande, voice lead at Silhouette, says being located in a shopping centre means more people can easily arrive by public transport and gives the group more visibility.

"We've had it before where people are like 'Oh, what's this? We don't know what this is.'

"That is how we can get other people to join us."

stories.summary: Applications are being denied despite a change to make it easier, Jersey Consumer Council says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Government of Jersey said whether credit cards were offered to islanders "remains a commercial decision"

Published 5 hours ago

Islanders are still struggling to get credit cards despite personal data changes to make it easier to apply for one, a consumer council has said.

The changes which came into force on 30 July meant the government could securely share personal data with UK credit reference agencies, which had been seen as the main barrier to successful applications .

However, the Jersey Consumer Council said several providers had still refused applications and called for the government to work closer with businesses and banks.

A spokesperson for Jersey's government said it had "engaged with providers throughout this process" and whether products were offered in the island "remains a commercial decision".

Carl Walker from the Jersey Consumer Council said credit card companies may need convincing to bring their business back

Carl Walker, from Jersey Consumer Council, said credit card companies would need to be reminded of the change which had allowed more information to be shared.

"The last time they were involved... Jersey was slamming the door shut, so they have switched off and turned their attention elsewhere," he said.

"We're pushing the government to write them an official letter to say this piece of legislation has now changed, Jersey's now open for business... and then leave it up to them whether they decide they to come back or not."

A spokesperson said the government had "successfully delivered a project to share islanders' data with credit reference agencies".

"This was a key issue identified by the industry as an obstacle to providing credit cards in Jersey," they said.

"It remains a commercial decision for providers to decide whether to offer their products or services, including credit cards, in Jersey.

stories.title: Wood Group offshore workers launch 48-hour strike in row over pay
stories.summary: The Unite union said workers had faced the threat of fire and rehire notices and of having their pay cut.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
At its peak in 2013, Wood reached a market valuation of more than £5bn and employed more than 50,000 people in oilfields around the world

Published 6 hours ago

Offshore workers on a number of North Sea platforms are taking strike action in a dispute over pay and conditions.

The Unite and RMT unions said they are in dispute with the Wood Group over its decision to "slash" the pay and conditions of dozens of offshore workers, including through the threat of issuing fire-and-rehire notices.

The strikes will affect a number of installations run by Harbour Energy, including the Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.

The Wood Group said it had been notified of the action and added that staff and operational safety remained its "top priority".

Production, instrument and mechanical technicians are among those set to walk out for a total of six days in October and November, beginning with a two-day walk-out which started at midnight.

Vic Fraser, Unite regional officer in Aberdeen, said his members had been left with no choice but to strike

Further walkouts are expected on 20 and 21 October and 3 and 4 November.

The RMT has also instructed its members not to work any overtime from 8 October until further notice.

The news comes after a warning that separate strike action by offshore workers at energy firm Apache could "severely disrupt" UK fuel supplies.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said: "Unite will not allow the Wood Group to slash and burn our members' pay and conditions.

"This is a profitable company and it is despicable that it is threatening to fire and rehire its workers. This is corporate greed in its worst form."

Vic Fraser, Unite industrial officer, said: "Industrial action will inevitably impact the operation of Harbour Energy's offshore assets.

"The workforce has been left with no option but to strike against the Wood Group's threats and intimidation.

"Our members are saying enough is enough."

Oil and gas giant Wood plc sold to Dubai engineering firm Published 17 November 2025

Financial watchdog launches probe into Wood Group Published 27 June 2025

RMT general secretary Eddie Dempsey said: "Our members are not asking for special treatment or unreasonable improvements.

"They are standing up to defend the terms and conditions they already have.

"Strike action is always a last resort, but our members have clearly shown that they are prepared to stand together to defend their livelihoods and the terms and conditions they have worked under for many years.

"Furthermore, instead of working with the union to resolve these issues, the company has inflamed the situation by threatening the use of fire-and-rehire tactics."

A Wood Group spokesperson said: "We have received notification of planned industrial action involving union members employed by Wood on one of our Harbour Energy contracts.

"This is in relation to a recent consultation on changes to employment terms and conditions with employees.

"Personnel and operational safety remain our top priority."

A Harbour Energy spokesperson said: "We are aware of discussions between Wood and its employees and we hope a constructive resolution can be reached.

"Our priority remains the safety of our people and assets.

"We continue to work closely with all our contractors and expect to maintain safe and reliable operations and production across our business."

stories.title: Community supermarket opens in shopping centre
stories.summary: Shoppers can access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries at the new social supermarket.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Gina English from the SEK Community Food Shop in Chatham says the store is open to everyone

Published 6 hours ago

A new community supermarket offering access to affordable and healthy food has opened in a Kent shopping centre.

The store run by SEK Community Food Shop welcomed the public to its home on the first floor of The Pentagon Centre in Chatham.

Gina English from SEK says the shop is open to all as "in addition to supporting people with food insecurity, people will also be able get wraparound support from us, help with employment, looking at CVs and interview skills. We're also going to help people with budgeting and money management and signposting to other local services".

Initial funding to set up the supermarket was provided by Medway Council through the Crisis and Resilience Fund.

Shoppers can walk straight into the social supermarket, with no prior booking required, to access a wealth of budget-friendly groceries, including a £1 fruit and vegetable bag.

Cost are kept low as the store redistributes surplus food to reduce waste, helping to protect the environment at the same time.

SEK already operates two similar stores in Kent.

English said: "We've had Ramsgate for about three years, Ashford just for just over a year and across the two shops in the last year alone we saw 55,500 transactions and we were able to save 170 tonnes of perfectly good food from going to waste, so they do work."

Rod Taffs and Shirley Graves from Chatham were among the first customers into the newly opened community supermarket

Some of the first to experienced the store were Shirley Graves and her partner Rod Taffs who have already filled their basket with bargains.

"People want to come down and see what they've got, it's amazing," says Graves.

"I've got a box of 20 samosas for £1.50 and a big huge bag of chicken for £6. Times are quite tight at the moment, being pensioners, it's cheap and the chicken is amazing."

"That's going to do us three or four meals," adds Taffs.

Medway Council leader, Vince Maple, said: "I think most people across Kent and Medway would want to see food not going to waste, so the ability to have good quality food at a reasonable price, helping not just our families and individuals on low incomes but helping all families has got to be a good thing."

The shop also has a confidential, soundproofed office pod at the back of the store where customers can seek personal advice and guidance.

The SEK Community Food Shop in The Pentagon Centre, Chatham, is open Monday to Saturday between 10:00 and 18:00.

stories.title: I'm a classic old-school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch
stories.summary: The Tory leader seeks to echo Margaret Thatcher as she sets out her guiding political principles.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 4 October 2026

Kemi Badenoch has declared herself a "classic old-school Conservative" as she begins her party's annual conference with a string of policy pledges and a 100 page statement on her guiding principles. , external

"I believe in common sense, people working hard and being rewarded for that effort," she told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg.

She added that welfare should be a "safety net, not a lifestyle".

The Tory leader is trying to ensure her party stands out in a crowded political field. The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in the opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than that of her party, has characterised Reform leader Nigel Farage as a "grumpy grandpa" and she told Laura Kuenssberg that Labour leader Andy Burnham is "the cheesy uncle who does all the dad jokes".

She described herself as a "no-nonsense mum".

Asked if her plan for benefit cuts and a massive increase in prison places was a return to the "nasty party" of the past, she said: "It's the common sense party. That's what we're doing.

"And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?"

In her essay The Right Way - a deliberate echo of an essay written by Margaret Thatcher in 1976 , external entitled The Right Approach - Badenoch says the last Conservative government failed because it did not know what it stood for.

Despite the party's rhetoric during its 14 years in power, she said: "We did little to reverse the structural changes Labour had made which took the country in the wrong direction.

"The result was that the state grew by stealth."

The essay says the "next Conservative government will have one central principle: business, not government, creates growth".

The Tories would achieve growth through tax cuts, cutting red tape and reducing the size of the civil service back to pre-pandemic levels, the essay says.

And it adds: "What is really missing from politics and government today is people prepared to say no.

"Political parties now need to recruit those who have the stomach to say no to good causes when the resources simply are not there to do everything."

An 88 foot long satirical take on the Bayeaux Tapestry poking fun at Labour and Reform UK is a popular attraction at the Tory conference

As their conference gets under way in Birmingham the Conservatives have pledged to end a childcare "cliff edge", which currently means parents earning more than £100,000 do not qualify for the entitlement.

The party has also promised to deliver 50,000 new prison places by slashing the overseas aid budget to £1bn a year in a bid to end the early release of offenders.

Over the 14 years the Conservatives were in power, around 500 net prison places were created, which takes into account 14,142 added in existing and new jails, set against 13,660 lost mainly to dilapidation and closures.

Speaking in the main conference hall, Badenoch sought to make the case that the party had moved on from 2024 and outlined her expectation that the next few days in Birmingham would be a chance for members to discuss their ideas.

She said: "We're going to be having debates, we're going to have arguments, they are going to be fun.

"We're going to challenge each other and afterwards we're still going to be a united party."

During a question and answer session, Badenoch focused on different topics covered in her essay – including citizenship and how communities need to operate on trust.

She said the UK is "not a dormitory, it is not a hotel" before speaking how "British culture means something".

To applause in the well-attended hall, Badenoch said: "I don't want lots of little ghettos of separatist communities where they are recreating the place they come from - that will ruin the United Kingdom."

Responding, Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said the Tory Party "is stuck in the past and remains completely out of touch with what people across Britain want to see".

"Last week Andy Burnham set out a plan to bring back hope to Britain. Kemi Badenoch wants to drag our country back to a politics that let so many people down over the past 40 years."

Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise

The average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer.

Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year.

In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets has increased expectations of a base rate rise .

Meanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level.

There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up the swap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages .

Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”.

She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.”

The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property.

Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February.

after newsletter promotion

There are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last week reporting that annual price growth had halved in September .

Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability. He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”

stories.title: 'Get on with the day job' - Welsh Tory leader attacks first minister's independence push
stories.summary: Darren Millar says Rhun ap Iorwerth has failed to improve public services or help Welsh businesses.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Darren Millar focused this year's speech on preserving the UK

Published 4 October 2026

The Welsh Conservative leader Darren Millar has told the first minister to "get on with the day job" instead of focusing on the prospect of independence at a speech on Sunday.

Darren Millar told the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham that "Britain needs Badenoch" and reaffirmed his party's support for the UK.

It comes after First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth called for a "new deal" for Wales from the UK government at a Plaid Cymru conference, and said at a rally there was "no turning back" on the independence journey.

Millar says his party was committed to keeping the UK together and that Britain's legacy should be used to inspire future generations.

Millar returned to the expanded 96-member Welsh Parliament after May's Senedd election with a group of seven Welsh Tory members - down nine on the previous parliament.

Polls at various points during the election campaign had suggested the party could face a wipe-out, in part because of the rise in popularity of Reform in Wales.

The Tories could nonetheless end up doing a deal to pass the Welsh government's budget - its spending plans for the next financial year - after holding talks with Plaid, which is running a minority administration and needs to do a deal with another party.

Ahead of the speech on Sunday, the Tory shadow Welsh secretary told BBC Wales Plaid would need to consider lowering taxes if it wanted her party's support.

Darren Millar has backed his party leader Kemi Badenoch to be the next prime minister

Millar said the Welsh government must focus on fixing public services and defend the relationship between the four countries of the UK - saying his party "will never allow" the break up of the union.

"A plan to draw a slate curtain between Wales and the rest of the UK will cause more harm than good for our children and future generations," he said.

He pointed to rising NHS waiting lists, claimed Welsh businesses had "continued to struggle" since Plaid came to power, and that ap Iorwerth had instead decided to "cosy up to the SNP and Sinn Fein" referencing the recent meeting in Cardiff between the three countries leaders.

"He then signed a pact to promote the break-up of our United Kingdom," he said.

"The whole jamboree was seized upon by Vladimir Putin's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov , who gleefully spoke up on Russian TV about the prospect of independence referendums across the UK.

"So my message to Rhun ap Iorweth today is this - get on with the day job."

Party leader Kemi Badenoch speaking at the conference

Referencing ap Iorwerth, Millar said: "He told voters in May that the Senedd election was not about independence.

"Well, either he didn't get his own memo or he deliberately chose to deceive people.

"Because just like the Pied Piper of Hamelin, the Plaid Piper of Anglesey has tried to hoodwink people."

Miller described the UK as "more than a political arrangement", saying each helped to develop industries, abolish the slave trade, liberate Europe and shape the modern world.

"We are a shared family of nations. For centuries, the people of Wales, England, Scotland and Northern Ireland have lived together, worked together and traded together.

"Of course, there are those on the left who say we should apologise or be embarrassed about our history.

"But I say that it is a legacy and a heritage that we should be proud of and use to inspire the next generation."

The Shadow Welsh Secretary Mims Davies branded a recent meeting of the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland a "separatist summit".

Davies was speaking at a discussion on the union at Conservative party conference in Birmingham.

She also claimed the Plaid Cymru Welsh government could not afford its flagship childcare policy.

"That has meant that families have been sold a pup," said Davies.

"It feels that if you're living in Wales, life is far too hard, and there is nobody really standing up for the people of Wales," the MP told delegates.

stories.summary: Russell Findlay tells the Conservative Party's UK conference that breaking up the United Kingdom would be "a gift to our enemies".

Russell Findlay said the SNP's talk of independence was dangerous

Published 4 October 2026

Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay has described the SNP's "obsession" with independence as "dangerously irresponsible".

First Minister John Swinney has said he wants to hold a second Scottish independence referendum by 2031, despite successive prime ministers refusing to countenance another poll.

Findlay told the Conservative Party's UK conference that while the United Kingdom continues to face "grave threats" from China, Russia and Iran, a divided UK would be "a gift to our enemies".

And he called on Swinney to respect the result of the 2014 referendum where a majority of Scots voted no to independence.

I'm a classic old school Conservative, says Kemi Badenoch Published 1 day ago

Swinney aiming for independence referendum by 2031 Published 14 September

PM says second Scottish independence referendum remains 'off limits' Published 10 September

Findlay told delegates: "We face Russian hostility in our waters and Iranian plots on our streets. These totalitarian regimes want a divided United Kingdom.

"And we have SNP politicians who share that aim. They want to shut down Faslane. They oppose Britain's armed forces. They would make us less safe.

"In today's volatile world, relentless SNP chatter about independence is no longer just a dangerous distraction. It is now dangerously irresponsible."

The Scottish Tory leader also used his speech to attack what he described as the SNP's "broken" benefits system.

He said the Scottish government's approach was trapping people in a life of misery on "Benefits Street" and also giving the green light to "chancers and crooks".

"My party values the safety net of social security, despite the tiresome anti-Tory tropes peddled by our rivals," Findlay said.

"But Scotland's benefits system under the SNP is broken. Around one pound of every seven spent by them goes on benefits.

"By 2031, Scotland's benefits bill will be more than £9bn. That's more than we spend on schools, universities, colleges, police, courts and prisons combined.

"Social security should be there for times of need, it shouldn't be a lifestyle choice."

Benefit fraud bill

Findlay said the Scottish Tories would launch a Benefit Fraud Bill to help recover overpayments.

"We will demand taxpayers' get their money back, instead of just asking nicely.

"Overpayments could be taken directly from bank accounts, as happens elsewhere in the UK.

"Driving licences could be confiscated if refunds are not forthcoming. Our law would double the maximum sentence for benefit fraud to 10 years.

"Benefits should be for those suffering genuine hardship.

"That would deliver true fairness, dignity and respect."

The Scottish Tory leader went on to criticise John Swinney for "cosying up to Sinn Fein" at a recent summit in Cardiff.

Findlay said: "Since Mr Swinney was a teenager, all he's cared about is breaking up the United Kingdom.

"Sorry Mr Swinney, and your new friends in Sinn Fein, but we won't let that happen.

"Let's not forget that Sinn Fein has never denounced the IRA slaughter of innocent men, women and children.

"Yet Mr Swinney works with them to destroy the United Kingdom. A disgrace."
